title: From a Family Clay Oven to a James Beard Nod: The Immigrant Story Behind Las Vegas's Hottest Indian Restaurant
excerpt: Tamba — named for the Hindi word for copper — earned a Best New Restaurant finalist nod from the James Beard Foundation in its first year, capping a three-decade journey that began with an immigrant couple's modest Monterey restaurant.
body:
In 1989, Daljit and Jatinder Dhillon opened a small restaurant called India's Clay Oven in Monterey, California. They were immigrants, still figuring out America, and their ambitions were modest: serve good food, build a life, raise a family. Three years later, they opened Gandhi India's Cuisine. When they eventually moved to Las Vegas, they brought the name Tamba — Hindi for copper, a metal sacred in Indian tradition, believed to purify water and bring good health — to a spot on the Strip, where it became a fixture of the city's culinary fabric for nearly two decades.

Then, in 2022, the Hawaiian Marketplace was demolished, and Tamba disappeared.

The story could have ended there — one more immigrant restaurant that served its community, thrived quietly, and vanished when the real estate changed. But the Dhillons' son, Sunny, who had spent three decades learning at his father's side, had other ideas. In late 2024, he brought Tamba back. Not as a nostalgia project, but as a reinvention.

## Six Fires, One Kitchen

The new Tamba, at Town Square in Las Vegas, is nothing like the original. The dining room evokes 1930s Art Deco Mumbai, with opulent architectural details that signal ambition. The kitchen is organised around six live-fire stations: a raw bar held at 38°F for sashimi and oysters, a charcoal mangal reaching 800°F for kebabs, a Josper oven pushing 1,000°F for steaks, a clay tandoor for naan and tikka, an Asian wok station exceeding 1,000°F, and a traditional curry station.

Leading this operation is Executive Chef Anand Singh, who was born in the Himalayan foothills of Uttarakhand and has cooked across six countries. His menu is what the restaurant calls "Contemporary Indian" — Indian cuisine that has travelled the world and found its home in Las Vegas. A pomelo salad that is sweet-tart, juicy, crunchy, and humming with chilli heat. Angara Wagyu — a fourteen-ounce Margaret River New York strip. Butter chicken reimagined: roasted in the tandoor, finished in makhani sauce.

The restaurant also features a sushi and raw bar programme led by Chef Sung Park, and Bar Jadu — a cocktail lounge serving twenty-seven handcrafted drinks.

## The James Beard Moment

In March 2026, the James Beard Foundation named Tamba a finalist for Best New Restaurant — one of the most competitive and prestigious categories in the annual awards, often called the Oscars of the food world. Las Vegas had garnered a record-breaking fourteen semifinalist nominations that year, but Tamba's inclusion was the one that carried the heaviest symbolism.

It was not just an Indian restaurant being honoured; it was an immigrant family's restaurant being honoured. The kind of place that starts with a clay oven and a prayer and, over three decades and two generations, becomes something that the country's most important culinary institution considers worthy of its highest stage.

"Tamba carries one of the most layered origin stories in Las Vegas dining," wrote the tourism authority Visit Las Vegas, noting that the restaurant "stands out for its restraint and for proving that tradition and innovation can coexist beautifully."

## The Diaspora Backdrop

Tamba's trajectory mirrors a larger shift in how Indian cuisine is perceived in America. For decades, Indian restaurants in the United States occupied a narrow band: casual neighbourhood spots offering buffet lunches and take-out curry. The new generation — Tamba, Ettan in Palo Alto, Musaafer in New York, Semma in Greenwich Village — is claiming space at the top of the fine-dining pyramid.

The James Beard Foundation's 2026 nominations underscore the point. Srijith Gopinathan and Ayesha Thapar of the Cal-India Collective (Ettan, Copra, Eylan, and Little Blue Door across four California cities) and Meherwan and Molly Irani of the Chai Pani Restaurant Group were both finalists for Outstanding Restaurateur. Indian cuisine has never had a year like this at America's most prestigious food awards.

For the estimated 4.8 million Indian Americans watching, the message is clear: the clay oven that Daljit and Jatinder Dhillon fired up in Monterey in 1989 was not the end of a journey. It was the beginning of one.

## What's Next

Tamba earned a AAA Four Diamond Award in 2026 — a designation given to fewer than two per cent of restaurants inspected by AAA. With an average rating of 4.7 across more than 850 reviews, it has become one of the highest-rated Indian restaurants in the United States. Seventy per cent of its menu is permanent signatures; thirty per cent rotates seasonally.

Sunny Dhillon has not announced plans for a second location, but the demand is unmistakable. The family that started with India's Clay Oven is now at the centre of a conversation about what American fine dining looks like in 2026. The answer, increasingly, looks like it involves a tandoor.
